pages.p:
You met the function shell in unit 1. Now let us use it properly. A **function** is a named block of code that you can run whenever you want. You write it once and **call** it as many times as you like.

The word in the brackets is a **parameter**: a name for an input. The value you pass when you call is the **argument**.
pages.tip: Writing the function does not run it. Only a call like «sayHi("Ana")» runs it.

pages.p: Separate parameters with commas. When you call the function, the arguments are matched **by position**: the first argument goes to the first parameter, the second to the second, and so on. So the order matters.
pages.tip: JavaScript does not check the order for you. Look at your function when you call it.

pages.p:
«return» sends a value back to the place where the function was called. It also **stops the function right away**. Any code after a «return» that runs is never reached.

A function with no «return» gives back «undefined».
pages.tip: When «n» is -5 the first «return» runs, so the second one is skipped.

pages.p: A call that returns a value can be used like any value: store it in a variable, do maths with it, or use it in an «if». Functions that answer yes or no, like «isEven», read very nicely in conditions.
pages.tip: Names like «isEven» or «isAdult» tell the reader that the function returns true or false.

pages.p: You can give a parameter a **default value** with «=». If the caller leaves that argument out, JavaScript uses the default. If the caller gives a value, that value wins.
pages.tip: Without a default, a missing argument becomes «undefined».

pages.p:
There is a shorter way to write a function: an **arrow function**. You store it in a «const». Write the parameters, then an arrow «=>», then the value to return.

When the part after the arrow is a single expression, it is returned automatically. You do not write «return».
pages.tip: You call an arrow function exactly like a normal one: «double(4)».

pages.p: If an arrow function needs several lines, use curly braces after the arrow. Now it works like a normal function body, so you must write «return» yourself. Forget it and you get «undefined».
pages.tip: Normal or arrow? Both are fine. In this course use whichever feels clearer.

pages.p: A function can call another function. This lets you build big jobs from small, simple pieces. Each small function has one job and a clear name.
pages.tip: 3 squared is 9 and 4 squared is 16. Together that is 25.

pages.p:
A variable made inside a function is **local**: it exists only while the function runs, and only inside that function. The area where a name can be used is called its **scope**.

Parameters are local too. Outside the function, «secret» below does not exist, and using it would give a «ReferenceError».
pages.tip: The function gave the value out with «return». The name «secret» stayed inside.

pages.p:
A variable made outside all functions is an **outer** (global) variable. A function can read it, and even change it if it was made with «let».

But changing outer variables inside a function makes code hard to follow. A good habit: send data in with parameters, and get data out with «return».
pages.tip: «console.log» can print several values. It puts a space between them.

pages.p:
If a parameter or a local variable has the same name as an outer variable, they are **two separate boxes**. The function uses its own box and the outer one stays untouched.

Numbers and text are **copied** into a parameter, so changing the parameter does not change the original.
pages.tip: Inside «change», «x» is 5 at first. The outer «x» is a different variable.

pages.p:
Good functions do **one job** and have a clear name. They return a result instead of printing it, so other code can use that result.

Here three small functions work together. Notice how «ticket» reads almost like English.
pages.tip: If a function is hard to name, it probably does too many jobs.

hand.why: The inner call «double(3)» gives 6. The outer call doubles that to 12.
The argument is the value you pass when calling. «name» is the parameter, the name that receives the value.
«show» prints A but has no «return», so it gives back «undefined». That is what «r» holds.

hand.q: Complete the function so it gives back three times the number.
hand.why: «return» sends the value back to the caller. Without it the function gives back «undefined».
No argument was passed, so the default value "friend" is used.
«square(4)» returns 16 and then 1 is added, so the result is 17.

hand.q: Put the lines in order so the program prints true.
hand.why: Define the function first, then call it. 6 divided by 2 leaves remainder 0, so the answer is true.
An arrow function puts «=>» between the parameters and the result.
The «x» inside «f» is a separate local variable. The outer «x» is still 1.

hand.q: Why does a function usually use «return» instead of «console.log» for its answer?
hand.ans: return gives the value back, so other code can use it
wrong: return makes the answer appear faster
console.log is not allowed inside functions
return prints the value in a nicer way
hand.why: «console.log» only shows a value to the person. «return» hands the value to the code that called the function, which can store it or use it in maths.
«return» ends the function immediately. The line after it is never reached.
«inc(5)» is 6 and «inc(6)» is 7. Calling one function from another is normal.

hand.q: What happens when this code runs?
hand.ans: It stops with ReferenceError: secret is not defined
hand.why: «secret» is local to the function. The last line is outside, where that name does not exist.
Without a second argument the default is used. 5 to the power 2 is 25.

hard.why: «minus(10, 2)» is 8 and «minus(2, 10)» is -8. Arguments go by position, so the order matters. 8 times -8 is -64.
After the first call «count» is 2. The second call makes it 4 and returns 4. Then «count» is read as 4 too, so 4 + 4 is 8.
The parameter «n» is a copy. Doubling it does not change the outer «n», which stays 5.
With one argument, «b» is 10, so the result is 11. With two arguments, «b» is 2, so the result is 3.
«sumTo(4)» is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The arrow function doubles it to 20.
For 20, the first square above 20 is 5 × 5 = 25, so the loop returns 5. For 500, no square up to 10 × 10 is above 500, so the loop ends and the function returns -1.
The line «a + b;» works out the sum but throws it away. With no «return», the function gives back «undefined».

hard.code:
const f = (a, b = 2) => a ** b;
console.log(f(3), f(2, 5));
hard.why: «f(3)» uses the default 2, so 3 ** 2 is 9. «f(2, 5)» is 2 to the power 5, which is 32.

hard.q: Complete the condition so the program prints teen.
hard.why: The «if» needs a true or false value. The call «isTeen(age)» returns exactly that.

hard.q: Put the lines in order so the program prints HEY!
hard.why: The function is defined first, then called with an argument and stored in «msg», and finally printed.

items.symptom: It prints undefined but it should print 8.
items.why: The function works out «n * 2» but never gives it back. It needs «return».

items.symptom: It should divide 10 by 2 and print 5, but it prints 0.2.
items.why: Arguments go to parameters by position. The first argument is «a», the number to divide.

items.symptom: It prints 12 and then NaN. It should print only 13.
items.why: «console.log» shows the area but returns nothing, so «undefined + 1» is NaN. «return» gives the value back.

items.symptom: ReferenceError: tax is not defined. It should print 110.
items.why: «tax» is local to the function. Outside, the name does not exist. The result is already returned.

items.symptom: It prints undefined but it should print 9.
items.why: With curly braces you must write «return». Without braces the value is returned automatically.

items.symptom: ReferenceError: squar is not defined. It should print 8.
items.why: The name is spelled wrong. JavaScript only knows «square».

project.title: Cinema Ticket
project.brief:
Write a function «ticketPrice(age, isWeekend)» that returns the price of a cinema ticket.

• younger than 5: free (0)
• age 5 to 12: 8
• age 65 or older: 10
• everyone else: 15

On the weekend, add 2 to the price, but free tickets stay free. Make «isWeekend» default to «false», so «ticketPrice(30)» works with one argument.

Examples: «ticketPrice(30)» is 15 and «ticketPrice(10, true)» is 10.
